Some nouns name a relation,
so they are incomplete without the thing they relate to.
Examples include:

- *cause* (of what?)
- *effect* (of what, on what?)
- *reason* (for what?)
- *result* (of what?)
- *example* (of what?)

When one of these nouns appears without its "of" or "for" phrase,
the reader has to recover the missing object from context,
just as with a pronoun that has no clear referent.
Write the object next to the noun.

::: {#exm-relational-noun}

## Comparing four versions of one sentence

Each version tries to say what usually causes garden-path sentences.

> 1. A common cause in technical writing is a clause that describes a noun
>    but has lost its opening *that* or *that were*.
> 2. In technical writing, a common cause is a clause that describes a noun
>    but has lost its opening *that* or *that were*.
> 3. In technical writing, a common cause of garden-path parsing is a clause
>    that describes a noun but has lost its opening *that* or *that were*.
> 4. A common cause of garden-path sentences in technical writing
>    is a clause that describes a noun
>    but has lost its opening *that* or *that were*.

Versions 1 and 2 never say what the clause causes,
so the reader has to look back for it.
Version 3 names it,
but its fronted phrase delays the subject
(see [Lead with the subject](conciseness.qmd#lead-with-the-subject)),
and "garden-path parsing" introduces a second term
for the "garden-path sentences" that the section defines.
Version 4 names the object, uses the defined term,
and starts with the subject.

:::
